name: The Wandering Continents: Pangaea and Beyond
description: Supercontinents that formed and split, oceans that opened and closed, and the long argument that proved the ground beneath us moves.

checkpoints.name: Early supercontinents
checkpoints.note: Geologists propose that the land gathered again and again into huge masses: Columbia, then Rodinia, then Pannotia and Gondwana. The Pacific Ocean is thought to have begun opening as Rodinia broke up, and the Iapetus Ocean lay between old continents.

checkpoints.name: Pangaea
checkpoints.note: The Rheic Ocean closed as continents collided, and in the late Paleozoic most land was joined in Pangaea, with the Tethys Ocean as a great gulf to its east.

checkpoints.name: The breakup
checkpoints.note: Pangaea split and the Atlantic opened along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. The Gulf of Mexico, Indian and Arctic oceans took shape, Zealandia broke from Gondwana and mostly sank, and India ran into Asia to raise the Himalayas and the Tibetan plateau.

checkpoints.name: The modern map
checkpoints.note: The Southern Ocean opened around Antarctica, Africa began to split along the East African Rift and the Red Sea, and what remained of the Tethys became the Mediterranean.

checkpoints.name: The idea that moved continents
checkpoints.note: Alfred Wegener argued in 1912 that continents drift, but few geologists believed him. Evidence from the sea floor in the 1950s and 1960s turned his idea into plate tectonics.
